text.hook:
Everyone uses std::mutex. Few can explain what it actually guarantees.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it for your next interview. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The three properties of a mutex
2. The UB traps and the four lock wrappers
3. What a blocked thread really does
4. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: why does a `const` getter that locks a member mutex need `mutable std::mutex`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: lock() is a non-const member function, so it cannot be called on a member of a const object. Locking is not a logical change to the object, so the mutex is declared mutable.

slides.lead: What a lock really guarantees, what it never promises, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: A mutex gives you three separate things

cards.label: Mutual exclusion
cards.text: At most one owner at a time.

cards.label: Ownership
cards.text: The thread that locked it is the one that must unlock it.

cards.label: Synchronization
cards.text: `unlock()` *synchronizes-with* the next `lock()`: writes before it are visible after it.

slides.takeaway: It does **not** give: thread order, fairness, or protection for any access made without the lock.

slides.title: Classic interview traps
rows: Unlock from a thread that is not the owner
Destroy a mutex while it is locked
Owner thread exits holding the lock
slides.takeaway: RAII guards remove all of these: the destructor unlocks on return, early return and exceptions.

slides.title: Which lock object?
rows: CV waits, early unlock, defer / try / timed, moving a lock out
Default choice. Locks 2+ mutexes without deadlock
slides.takeaway: All are exclusive except `shared_lock`. `unique_lock` is the *flexible* one, not the more exclusive one.

slides.kicker: glibc / Linux, not a C++ guarantee
slides.title: What a blocked thread actually does
steps: Fast path: one CAS on the lock word, 0 ➜ 1. Pure user space, no syscall.
Contended: mark the word "locked with waiters" (2), then `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)`: the thread sleeps, using no CPU.
Unlock: store 0. Only if waiters existed: `futex(FUTEX_WAKE, 1)`.
The woken thread must re-compete. A running thread may barge in first: no FIFO.

slides.hero:
An uncontended mutex is cheap.
Contention is what you design against.
slides.lead: Uncontended: a couple of user-space atomics. Contended: serialization (one core does the work) and tail latency.

slides.title: Never hold a lock across
items: I/O, or logging to a file or socket
slides.takeaway: Snapshot pattern: copy the shared state under the lock, release, then do the slow work on the private copy.

items.myth: "Every mutex lock is a system call."
items.truth: Uncontended lock and unlock are user-space atomics. The kernel is only used to sleep and wake waiters.

items.myth: "The thread that started first gets the mutex first."
items.truth: No ordering, no FIFO, no fairness.
Only the owner. Use a semaphore for cross-thread signalling.

items.myth: "When a thread finishes, its mutexes are released."
items.truth: A thread exiting while it owns a `std::mutex` is UB. In practice (glibc) it simply stays locked.

items.myth: "`unique_lock` is the exclusive one, `lock_guard` is not."
items.truth: Both are exclusive. `unique_lock` is the flexible one.
Only when read sections are long enough to amortize its overhead. Fairness is implementation-defined.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Every increment is "locked". Two threads, 100000 each.

Is this code correct? What does it print?
Think it through, comment your answer, then swipe ➜
text.body: One missing word changes everything. The compiler even tells you, if you read the warning.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: what does `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>{mtx};` (braces, no name) do inside the loop? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: It creates a temporary that locks and unlocks at the end of that statement, so `++counter` still runs unlocked. Always name the guard.

slides.title:
Every increment is "locked".
What is printed?

bullets: It declares a new, default-constructed `unique_lock` named `mtx`, shadowing the global mutex. It owns nothing.
Output is unpredictable: at `-O2` it often prints 200000 anyway (the loop folds into one `+= 100000`), at `-O0` about 100000.

slides.title: Give the guard a name
slides.tip: GCC warns: "unnecessary parentheses in declaration of 'mtx'". Read it as "this is a declaration, not a lock". The `lock_guard` version of this mistake does not even compile (no default constructor).

text.hook:
T1 is started first. Both threads lock the same mutex.
So T1 always prints first. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Most answers assume some kind of queue. The standard promises less than you think.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: what does `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m, std::adopt_lock);` do to `m`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: It never locks. It assumes this thread already owns m and only takes over the unlock. Used on a mutex you do not own, it unlocks an unowned mutex: UB.

slides.title:
T1 is started first.
Which line prints first?

slides.verdict_sub: One x86-64 Linux machine: `T2` printed first in 704 of 2000 runs
bullets: Creation order says nothing about scheduling. Whoever reaches `lock()` first wins.
`std::mutex` promises exclusion. No FIFO queue, no fairness.
glibc: unlock wakes one sleeper, but a running thread can grab the lock first (barging).
Unfair locks are faster, at the cost of possible starvation.

slides.title: Need an order? Build it explicitly
slides.tip: Also: `join()`, a CV with a predicate, a semaphore, a release/acquire flag. A ticket lock gives FIFO at a throughput cost.
slides.takeaway: Mutex = exclusion, not ordering and not fairness.

text.hook:
A reader finds the key missing, so it "upgrades" to a write lock.

Only one thread runs. Can this deadlock?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This read-then-upgrade pattern looks natural in a cache. Slide 3 shows the version that is safe.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: suppose `shared_mutex` did support upgrades. Two readers try to upgrade at the same time. What happens? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: They deadlock each other: each waits for the other to release its shared ownership. That is why no upgrade operation is offered.

slides.title:
One thread only.
Can this deadlock?

slides.verdict_sub: glibc: prints the "upgrading" line, then hangs. Self-deadlock, formally UB
bullets: The exclusive lock waits until **all** shared owners release.
The thread itself is still a shared owner, and it is now blocked. It waits for itself forever.

slides.title: Release, lock exclusively, re-check
slides.tip: Re-check: a writer may insert the key in the gap. `try_emplace` handles it.
slides.takeaway: Shared to exclusive: release, acquire, re-check.

text.hook:
"A mutex always goes through the kernel, so it is slow."
One thread, a million lock/unlock pairs. Count the syscalls.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The real answer explains why an uncontended lock is cheap and a contended one is not.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: a getter locks the mutex and returns a `const std::string&` to a member. Is the caller's read protected? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. The lock is released when the getter returns, so the caller reads the member unlocked while a writer may modify it: a data race. Return a copy made under the lock.

slides.title:
Linux, glibc, one thread.
How many syscalls does the loop make?

slides.verdict_sub: `strace -c` (glibc, x86-64): no syscalls from the loop
bullets: Uncontended lock: CAS the lock word 0 ➜ 1 in user space. Done.
Uncontended unlock: set it back to 0. No waiters, no kernel.
The kernel is involved only when a thread must sleep or be woken (`futex` on Linux).
Uncontended, a mutex costs about two atomic RMWs.

slides.title: glibc's scheme, simplified
slides.takeaway: Uncontended: user-space atomics. Contended: may sleep via a futex. 0/1/2 is glibc's design, not C++.

text.hook:
p50 latency is normal. p99.9 jumps to milliseconds.
Tracing points at a report holding the stats mutex.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A classic low-latency design question. The tempting answer fixes the wrong thing.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: 12 threads share one `unordered_map` behind a global mutex. CPU sits at 50% but latency is high. What do you redesign? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Shard by key (hash(key) % N, one cache-line-padded mutex per shard), or better, route each shard to a single owning thread so it needs no lock at all.

slides.title:
`report()` holds the lock 5 to 8 ms.
Best fix?
options: A read lock for the report
A timed lock on the hot path

slides.verdict_sub: The lock is not slow. The hold time is.
bullets: Most events never meet a report. The few that do wait ms: only the tail suffers.
Spinlock: still waits the full 5 to 8 ms, and burns a core.
Reader/writer lock (`shared_mutex`): the hot path *writes*, so it still waits.
Timed lock (`timed_mutex`): the hot path still waits, then must drop or defer work.

slides.title: Lock for one copy, not for the report
slides.tip: Better still: the hot path publishes snapshots or events to the reporter through a queue.
slides.takeaway: Never hold a lock across I/O, logging, allocation or callbacks. Shorten hold time, do not change the lock type.
